pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 2: Technology in the Community

Technology is changing how we learn, work and live in our communities. In this unit you will discover digital tools that make learning in every subject easier and more exciting. You will also look honestly at the harm careless computer use can do to our environment, especially through electronic waste, and propose ways your community can reduce it. You will finish by turning discarded computer parts into something useful.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.1.2.1** Demonstrate the use of technology in the community.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.1.2.1.1** Describe and give examples of at least five technology tools for learning in each subject.
- **B7.1.2.1.2** Demonstrate the use of at least three technology tools identified.
- **B7.1.2.1.3** Discuss the benefits of using technology tools in learning.
- **B7.1.2.1.4** Examine the negative impact of computers and computer use on the environment.
- **B7.1.2.1.5** Propose environmentally responsible practices to reduce the negative impact of computers.
- **B7.1.2.1.6** Create a component from disposed computer parts.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 2.1 Technology Tools for Learning
- 2.2 Demonstrating Technology Tools
- 2.3 Benefits of Technology Tools in Learning
- 2.4 Negative Impact of Computers on the Environment
- 2.5 Environmentally Responsible Computing
- 2.6 Creating Something New from Disposed Computer Parts

**Core competencies developed:** Digital Literacy (DL5.3), Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1).

pages.title: Technology Tools for Learning
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe at least five technology tools for learning in each subject;
- give examples of how each tool supports learning.
A **technology tool for learning** is any hardware, software, app or website that helps you understand, practise, create or share knowledge. Some tools are general (they help in every subject); others are designed for one subject.
## General tools that support every subject
| **Tool** | **Examples** | **How it helps learning** |
|---|---|---|
| Word processor | Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer | Write and edit essays, notes and reports; check spelling |
| Spreadsheet | Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, LibreOffice Calc | Record data, calculate, draw graphs |
| Presentation software | PowerPoint, Google Slides, Canva | Present projects with pictures, charts and video |
| Online encyclopaedias and search engines | Google, Bing, Wikipedia, Britannica | Research any topic quickly |
| Virtual Learning Environments | Google Classroom, Moodle, Microsoft Teams | Receive notes, submit assignments and take quizzes online |
| Open learning websites | Khan Academy, BBC Bitesize, Coursera | Free lessons, videos and practice at your own pace |

pages.title: Tools for specific subjects
pages.body:
## Tools for specific subjects
| **Subject** | **Technology tools (at least five)** |
|---|---|
| Mathematics | **Spreadsheets** (tables, formulas, graphs); **GeoGebra** (geometry and graphs); **Desmos** (graphing calculator); scientific calculators; **Khan Academy** practice exercises; Mathigon / Math Playground puzzles |
| Science | **PhET Interactive Simulations** (virtual experiments); virtual laboratories; **Google Earth** (landforms, weather); digital microscopes; data loggers and sensors; science videos (e.g. NASA, BBC) |
| English Language | Word processors with spelling and grammar check; online dictionaries and thesaurus; **Scrabble** and other word games; e-books and audiobooks; typing tutors; speech-to-text |
| Social Studies & History | **Virtual museums** (Google Arts & Culture virtual tours); Google Earth and Maps; timeline makers; online newspapers; documentary videos; census and population data in spreadsheets |
| Computing | **Scratch**; **Lightbot**; Code.org; Python (IDLE, Thonny); Tinkercad (3D design and circuits); typing tutors |
| Creative Arts & Design | Paint, GIMP, Canva, Inkscape (graphics); Audacity (audio recording); video editors (Clipchamp, CapCut); 3D modelling |
| Career Technology | CAD software (SketchUp, Tinkercad); spreadsheets for budgets; online recipe and nutrition calculators; simulation games |
| Ghanaian Language & French | Online dictionaries; Duolingo (French); recorded pronunciation videos; keyboard layouts for Ghanaian characters (ɛ, ɔ, ŋ) |

pages.title: Tools for specific subjects (continued)
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know?** **Scratch** was created at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). It is free, works in a web browser or as an offline app, and lets you build games and animations by snapping coloured blocks together. You will use it in Strand 4.
> 🧪 **Activity — Brainstorm**
With your teacher, brainstorm or search the Internet for technology tools you could use in **each** of your subjects. Record at least five per subject in a table and share the table with the class.

pages.title: Demonstrating Technology Tools
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- demonstrate the use of at least three technology tools for learning;
- present how a tool works to the whole class.
In this lesson, groups demonstrate three tools. Use the guides below, then present your tool to the class.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Tool 1: Using a spreadsheet to draw a graph of class test scores (Excel)**
1. Open Excel. In cell A1 type Name, in B1 type Score. Enter five learners’ names and scores in A2:B6.
2. Select the range A1:B6 by dragging over it.
3. Click **Insert › Charts › Column** (Clustered Column).
4. Click the chart title and type B7 Computing Test Scores.
5. Observe: the graph shows at a glance who scored highest and lowest, which would take longer to see from a list.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Tool 2: Exploring a virtual museum (Google Arts & Culture)**
1. Open a web browser and go to artsandculture.google.com.
2. Search for a museum or a topic, e.g. “Ghana”, “kente” or “ancient Egypt”.
3. Open a **Street View** museum tour and use the arrows to “walk” through the galleries. Zoom in on objects to read their descriptions.
4. Write three facts you learnt and the name of the museum.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Tool 3: Creating a simple animation in Scratch**
1. Go to scratch.mit.edu and click **Create** (or open the offline Scratch app).
2. From the **Events** category, drag the block when green flag clicked into the coding area.
3. From **Motion**, attach move 10 steps; from **Control**, wrap it in a forever block; from **Motion**, add if on edge, bounce.
4. Click the **green flag**. The cat sprite moves across the stage and bounces back. Click the red stop sign to end.
5. Change the number of steps and observe what happens.

pages.title: Demonstrating Technology Tools (continued)
pages.body:
> 💻 **Practical session — Group demonstration**
Each group selects one of the tools above, or another tool from Lesson 2.1, practises using it and gives a three-minute demonstration to the class explaining **what the tool is**, **how it works** and **how it helps learning**.

pages.title: Benefits of Technology Tools in Learning
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss the benefits of using technology tools in learning.
| **Benefit** | **Example** |
|---|---|
| Makes abstract ideas visible | A PhET simulation shows how electric current flows, which cannot be seen in real life. |
| Saves time and improves accuracy | A spreadsheet totals 200 scores and draws a graph in seconds without mistakes. |
| Access to rich information | Learners in a rural school can tour a world-famous museum or watch a science video. |
| Learning at your own pace | Khan Academy lets you replay a lesson until you understand it. |
| Increases interest and motivation | Games, animations and instant feedback make practice enjoyable. |
| Supports collaboration | Groups edit the same Google Doc or slide deck from different places. |
| Develops 21st-century skills | Using digital tools builds digital literacy, creativity and problem-solving needed for future jobs. |
| Supports learners with special needs | Text-to-speech, screen magnifiers and captions help learners with visual or hearing impairments. |
> 💡 **Think About It** Technology also has challenges: unreliable electricity and Internet, cost of devices and data, distraction from social media, and the risk of copying work without understanding (plagiarism). How can your school reduce these challenges?

pages.title: Benefits of Technology Tools in Learning (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity — Think–Pair–Share**
In pairs, discuss how using a spreadsheet to draw graphs in Mathematics or Science helps learning. List at least four benefits and share with another pair.

pages.title: Negative Impact of Computers on the Environment
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- observe how people use and dispose of computers in the community;
- describe the negative impacts of computers and computer use on the environment.
Computers bring many benefits, but producing, using and throwing them away can harm the environment and human health.
## 1. Electronic waste (e-waste)
**E-waste** (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment, WEEE) is any discarded electrical or electronic device: old computers, monitors, phones, chargers, batteries, printers and cables. E-waste is one of the fastest-growing kinds of waste in the world. Computers contain **toxic substances**:
| **Substance** | **Found in** | **Harm** |
|---|---|---|
| Lead | Old CRT monitor glass, solder on circuit boards | Damages the brain and nervous system, especially in children |
| Mercury | Backlights of older flat screens, some switches | Damages the brain, kidneys and unborn babies; poisons fish |
| Cadmium | Rechargeable batteries, old circuit boards | Damages kidneys and bones; can cause cancer |
| Brominated flame retardants | Plastic casings and cable insulation | Release dioxins when burnt; disrupt hormones |
| Lithium (in batteries) | Laptop and phone batteries | Can catch fire or explode if crushed or burnt |

pages.title: 2. Unsafe recycling and burning
pages.body:
## 2. Unsafe recycling and burning
In informal scrapyards, people often **burn cables and plastic** to recover copper, and break devices with stones and hammers. The smoke releases poisonous gases (dioxins and furans) into the air; toxic ash and acids seep into soil and water bodies, and workers, many of them young, suffer burns, breathing problems and poisoning.
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection — Agbogbloshie, Accra** For many years, the **Agbogbloshie** scrapyard (Old Fadama) near Accra’s Korle Lagoon was one of the best-known informal e-waste processing sites in West Africa, where cables were burnt in the open air. The site was demolished by the authorities in **2021**, but informal e-waste processing continues in other parts of the country. Ghana’s **Hazardous and Electronic Waste Control and Management Act, 2016 (Act 917)** and its regulations (**L.I. 2250**) control how e-waste is imported, collected and recycled, and introduced an **advance eco-levy** on imported electrical and electronic equipment.
## 3. Energy use and climate change
Computers, servers and data centres use a lot of electricity. In many countries electricity is produced by burning fossil fuels, which release **carbon dioxide (CO₂)**, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. Leaving computers, monitors and projectors on when not in use wastes energy and money.

pages.title: 4. Other impacts
pages.body:
## 4. Other impacts
- **Mining of raw materials** such as copper, gold, cobalt and coltan damages land and rivers (in Ghana, illegal mining, galamsey, pollutes water bodies).
- **Paper waste** from unnecessary printing leads to the cutting down of trees.
- **Heat and noise** from many machines in one room; packaging waste (plastics and polystyrene).
> 🧪 **Activity — Community observation**
1. Observe people who use and work with computers in your community (a computer repairer, an Internet café, a phone shop). Note what they do with broken devices and old batteries.
2. Watch a video or view pictures of how computers and other electronic devices are disposed of.
3. In groups, discuss the impact of what you observed on the environment and on people’s health. Present your findings.

pages.title: Environmentally Responsible Computing
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.5
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss how the negative effects of computers can be reduced;
- evaluate environmentally responsible practices;
- propose measures to manage e-waste in a particular environment.
[[fig:c7-f10|Figure 9: The 5R approach to responsible e-waste management]]
## Practices individuals and schools can adopt
| **Practice** | **How it helps** |
|---|---|
| Switch off or use Sleep mode | Turn off computers, monitors and projectors at the end of the day; set screens to sleep after a few minutes. Saves electricity and reduces CO₂. |
| Buy energy-efficient equipment | Look for the **ENERGY STAR** label or similar ratings; laptops generally use less power than desktops. |
| Print responsibly | Print only when necessary, preview before printing, print on both sides, and reuse scrap paper for rough work. |
| Extend the life of devices | Use protective cases, keep devices cool and clean, and upgrade RAM or replace a battery instead of buying a new device. |
| Repair, donate or resell | Working devices can be refurbished and given to schools or community centres. |
| Use licensed e-waste recyclers | Hand old devices to registered collectors or manufacturer take-back programmes. **Never burn** cables, boards or batteries. |
| Recycle batteries separately | Keep used batteries in a labelled container and send them for safe recycling. |

pages.title: Evaluating responsible practices
pages.body:
## Evaluating responsible practices
When evaluating a practice, ask: Is it **effective** (does it really reduce harm)? Is it **affordable**? Is it **practical** for our community? Does it protect **people’s health and jobs**?
> ✏️ **Worked example — Proposed e-waste plan for a community such as Agbogbloshie**
- Set up **designated collection points** where people can drop off e-waste safely and receive a small payment (buy-back).
- Train informal recyclers to dismantle devices with **protective equipment** (gloves, masks, goggles) and give them **cable-stripping machines** so they do not need to burn cables.
- Enforce **Act 917** and stop the import of non-working devices disguised as second-hand goods.
- Run **awareness campaigns** on radio, in schools and in churches/mosques about the health dangers of burning e-waste.
- Partner with licensed recycling companies to recover metals safely and export hazardous parts for proper treatment.
> 🧪 **Activity — Debate**
Debate the motion: “Ghana should ban the importation of all used (second-hand) computers.” Consider the benefits (cheaper devices for learners) and the problems (more e-waste).

pages.title: Creating Something New from Disposed Computer Parts
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.6
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- collect disposed computer and electronic parts safely;
- explain how computer parts are recycled;
- design and create a useful component from disposed parts.
**Upcycling** means turning waste into something of greater value. Many old computer parts can be reused creatively, keeping them out of landfills and scrapyards.
## How computer parts are recycled
1. **Collection** of old devices.
2. **Sorting and testing**: working parts are reused.
3. **Manual dismantling**: separating plastics, metals, glass, batteries and circuit boards.
4. **Shredding** of materials into small pieces.
5. **Separation** of metals (with magnets, water and air currents) from plastics.
6. **Recovery** of copper, gold, silver and aluminium in specialised, controlled facilities.
7. **Safe disposal** of hazardous leftovers.
## Project ideas
| **Disposed part** | **What you can create** |
|---|---|
| Old keyboard keys | Key-rings, letter magnets, a name plaque or a mosaic picture |
| Hard disk platters (opened by the teacher) | Wall clock face, coasters or decorative mirror |
| CDs / DVDs | Mosaic art, sun-catchers, bird scarers for farms, coasters |
| Computer mouse | Phone stand, a model car body, or a toy |
| Circuit boards (with batteries removed) | Picture frames, bookmarks, wall art |
| Old cases and fans | Pen holder, small storage box, a model robot |
| Working parts from several broken PCs | With the teacher, assemble **one working computer** for the class library |

pages.title: Creating Something New from Disposed Computer Parts (continued)
pages.body:
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Before you start**
- Work only under your teacher’s supervision and wear **gloves**.
- **Never open** old CRT monitors, power supply units or microwave parts: they can hold a dangerous electric charge long after being unplugged.
- **Remove batteries** first and keep them in a separate container; never puncture, crush or burn them.
- Do not burn or melt any plastics or cables. Wash your hands after the activity.
> 🧪 **Activity — Create a component**
1. Collect disposed computer or electronic parts from your home or community (with permission).
2. Watch a video or look at pictures showing how computer parts are recycled.
3. In groups, sketch a design, list your materials and tools, then build your component.
4. Present your product: what it is, which parts you used, and how it helps the environment.

pages.body:

## Short answer questions

3. Explain **three** ways computers harm the environment.
4. Explain the 5Rs of e-waste management.
5. Propose **four** measures to manage e-waste effectively in your community.
6. State **three** safety precautions when working with disposed computer parts.
